Then the measured value is --

\opt{A}{3.66 cm}
\opt{B}{3.55 cm}
\opt{C}{3.65 cm}
\opt{D}{3.56 cm}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

The universal gravitational constant is measured experimentally using Cavendish's experiment. This experiment is a very precise experiment which gives the value of G as $(6.6742\pm0.0010)\times10^{-11}$ N.m$^2$/kg$^2$. Since the universal gravitational constant has some error in it, using it if we find escape speed and acceleration due to gravity on Earth's surface, our values will have error in it. (Assume mass of Earth = $6.0000\times10^{24}$ kg \& radius of Earth = $6.4000\times10^6$ m.) What will be the maximum percentage error in calculating the escape speed on Earth ? (The measurement of mass of Earth has an error of 0.01 \% and radius of Earth has an error of 0.02\% ):-
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{0.045\%}
\opt{B}{0.0225 \%}
\opt{C}{0.015 \%}
\opt{D}{0.0025\%}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

Ram performs optical bench experiment to find out the focal length of a concave lens. For this purpose, he first takes a convex lens and measures the position of object needle and image needle. Then he combines convex lens and concave lens and again measures the object needle and image needle position. The optical bench has no bench error. The readings obtained by Ram in the two experiments are shown in the table below.
\begin{center}\small\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\begin{tabular}{|p{1.9cm}|c|c|c|}\hline
 & Object needle & Lens & Image needle\\ \hline
Convex lens & 37.1 cm & 50.6 cm & 77.6 cm\\ \hline
Convex and Concave lens & 37.1 cm & 50.6 cm & 91.1 cm\\ \hline
\end{tabular}\end{center}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The focal length of the convex lens is 9.0 cm.}
\opt{B}{The focal length of the concave lens is 81 cm in modulus.}
\opt{C}{The error in focal length of convex lens is approximately 0.1 cm.}
\opt{D}{The error in focal length of concave lens is approximately 1.0 cm.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

An air bubble under explosion inside water oscillates with a time period given by $T=P^aE^bd^c$ where `$P$' is pressure of air, `$E$' is energy of explosion, `$d$' density of liquid then :-
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$a=-5/6$}
\opt{B}{$b=-0.4\,a$}
\opt{C}{$c=0.5$}
\opt{D}{None of these}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=TOPS02-P2-PHY-S2-Q06, source={TOPS - Test 02 (28 Aug 2022)}, paper=2, qno=6, type=numerical, subtopic={Units and dimensions}, answer={6.50}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: dimensional analysis, numerical constants | steps: powers of h, c and r by dimensions; formula for the force per area; substitute the values; solve for k | Casimir force}]
Attraction between two uncharged conducting parallel plates placed in vacuum is described by Casimir effect. This force per unit area of each plate depends on plank's constant ($h$), speed of light ($c$) and separation between the plates ($r$). Using dimensional analysis, the dimensionless proportionality constant is `$k$'. If the force acting on $1\times1$ cm plates separated by 1 $\mu$m is 0.013 dyne, calculate the value of constant $k$ is $P\times10^{-3}$. The value of $P$ is
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=TOPS05-P2-PHY-S2-Q09, source={TOPS - Test 05 (14 Jan 2023)}, paper=2, qno=9, type=multi, subtopic={Units and dimensions}, answer={C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: dimensional analysis, fundamental quantities | steps: dimensions of each in M L T; solve for L and T in F P M; check}, also_in={Star Review (Other) - Test 01 (12 Sep 2022) P1 Q3}]
If force ($F$), momentum ($P$) and mass ($M$) are fundamental quantities in system of units, then dimensional formulae for length ($L$) and time ($T$) will be :-
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$[T]=\left[F^2P^{-1}M^0\right]$}
\opt{B}{$[L]=\left[F^{-1}M^{-2}P^{-1}\right]$}
\opt{C}{$[L]=\left[F^{-1}P^2M^{-1}\right]$}
\opt{D}{$[T]=\left[F^{-1}P^1M^0\right]$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\section*{TMAS papers}
\begin{bankq}[id=TMAS04-P1-PHY-S1-Q02, source={TMAS - Test 04 (19 Nov 2023)}, paper=1, qno=2, type=single, subtopic={Errors and measurement}, answer={C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I2 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: errors in a linear fit | steps: slope in terms of tension and density; frequency; propagate the errors}]
In an experiment to study standing waves, you use a string whose mass per length is $\mu=(1.0\pm0.1)\times10^{-4}$ kg/m. You look at the fundamental mode, whose frequency $f$ is related to the length $L$ and tension $T$ of the string by the following equation $L=\dfrac{1}{2f}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$. You make a plot with $L$ on the $y$-axis and $\sqrt T$ on the $x$-axis, and find that the best fitting line is $y=(8.0\pm0.3)\times10^{-3}x+(0.2\pm0.04)$ in SI units. What is the value of the frequency of the wave (including the error)? Express your result in SI unit (Hz).
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$6250\pm859.8$ Hz}
\opt{B}{$1250\pm32.3$ Hz}
\opt{C}{$6250\pm546.9$ Hz}
\opt{D}{$4875\pm287$ Hz}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=TMAS04-P1-PHY-S2-Q11, source={TMAS - Test 04 (19 Nov 2023)}, paper=1, qno=11, type=multi, subtopic={Errors and measurement}, answer={A,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: errors in repeated readings | steps: mean; absolute errors; percentage error}]
The period of oscillation of a simple pendulum in an experiment is recorded as $2.63$ sec, $2.56$ sec, $2.42$ sec, $2.71$ sec and $2.80$ sec respectively:-
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Time period is $2.62$ sec}
\opt{B}{Average absolute error is $0.01$ sec}
\opt{C}{Percentage error is $2.4\%$}
\opt{D}{Percentage error is $4.2\%$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\end{bankq}

The diameter of the cylinder is (in mm) :
\end{bankq}
